title: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy Unmasked by Teclistamab in a Refractory Multiple Myeloma Patient
case_prompt:
A 72-year-old man with kappa light chain–restricted multiple myeloma and high-risk cytogenetics (including TP53 deletion) presented with fever, confusion, and new-onset right upper- and lower-extremity weakness one week after receiving the first step‐up dose of teclistamab (0.06 mg/kg). His history included penta-refractory disease after multiple lines of therapy, prior spinal cord compression at T6 treated with laminectomy and radiotherapy, and ongoing maintenance immunosuppression. On presentation, his temperature was 100.4 °F, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were normal, and exam revealed disorientation and worsened right-sided weakness compared with his baseline. He tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 but had no respiratory symptoms and received a 3-day course of remdesivir.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated multiple new regions of white matter hypoattenuation without infarction or hemorrhage. On hospital day 3, brain MRI showed extensive confluent multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal abnormalities predominantly in the bilateral frontal lobes and left parietal lobe with corresponding areas of restricted diffusion, and there was no contrast enhancement. By day 4, his motor weakness and sensory deficits (proprioception and vibration) in the lower extremities had progressed. 

On day 5, lumbar puncture revealed CSF glucose 54 mg/dL, protein 80 mg/dL, 1 RBC, 2 nucleated cells (68% lymphocytes, 32% monocytes), and negative Gram stain, fungal and mycobacterial cultures. CSF PCRs for Varicella-Zoster virus, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, and CMV were negative. CSF VDRL and cryptococcal antigen were negative, and PCR for BK virus in blood and CSF was negative. A routine EEG showed diffuse slowing without seizures or epileptiform discharges.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke was considered because of focal deficits, but “MRI findings of multifocal white matter lesions were atypical for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, which usually presents with localized vascular lesions.”  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis was considered due to multifocal lesions, but “While CVST can cause multifocal lesions, the detection of JC virus in the CSF and the clinical course pointed towards PML over thrombosis.”  
3. CNS involvement from multiple myeloma was considered, but “CNS involvement from MM is rare, and the MRI findings were not characteristic of metastatic lesions.”  
4. Viral encephalitis was considered in the setting of immunosuppression, but “Although viral encephalitis can manifest with multifocal lesions, the CSF detection of the JC virus and clinical presentation better aligned with PML.”  
5. COVID-19–related encephalopathy was considered given concurrent infection, but “COVID-19 encephalopathy remained a consideration, but the JC virus detection and MRI findings were more specific for PML.”  
6. Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in adults (MIS-A) was considered, but “MIS-A can involve neurological complications, but the CSF and MRI results indicated PML as the more probable cause.”
